questions.q: How does this lesson's scope differ from Security & Access Controls Chapters 1-6?
options: Those chapters taught the security mechanics themselves; this lesson teaches the standing, instance-wide policy that governs how every team applies those mechanics
This lesson re-teaches ACL syntax and SSO configuration from scratch
Security & Access Controls only covered encryption, nothing else
There is no real difference between the two courses' content
questions.explain: The Technical Architect's job is setting the standing strategy, not re-learning the ACL/SSO/encryption mechanics already covered in course 10.

questions.q: Why is a single well-designed ACL not enough at enterprise architecture scale?
options: Without a shared role-naming and ACL-structure convention across teams, the instance becomes impossible to audit even if every individual ACL is correct
A single ACL can never be correctly designed
ACLs only apply to one table at a time, so scale is irrelevant
Enterprise scale requires removing ACLs entirely
questions.explain: Fifty teams each inventing their own naming and logic conventions makes 'who can see this table' unanswerable without reading every ACL by hand.

questions.q: What is the Technical Architect's specific responsibility in the enterprise SSO/Identity Provider decision?
options: Making sure ServiceNow's SAML/OIDC configuration and session policy align with the enterprise-wide IdP standard already chosen for the whole application portfolio
Independently choosing a different Identity Provider for ServiceNow than the rest of the organization uses
Disabling SSO entirely so each department manages its own logins
The CTA has no role in SSO decisions at all
questions.explain: The enterprise IdP choice is made once at the organization level; the CTA's job is aligning ServiceNow's configuration to it, not re-deciding it per instance.

questions.q: What does a real data-encryption strategy look like, according to this lesson?
options: A standing classification policy (e.g. SSNs and payment data always get column-level encryption) applied automatically to new fields, not a judgment call made per field as requests come in
Encrypting every field on the instance regardless of sensitivity
Deciding encryption case-by-case each time a team requests it, with no written policy
Avoiding encryption entirely to keep performance high
questions.explain: Deciding the policy once, by data category, means a new table is classified and encrypted correctly by default instead of reinventing 'sensitive' every time.

questions.q: Where does a security architecture strategy decision typically get captured, per this lesson and Lesson 3?
options: In an Architecture Decision Record, enforced through architecture review of new scoped applications
Nowhere — it's left as an unwritten understanding among the original team
Only inside a single scripted ACL's code comments
In the end-user training materials, not in any architecture document
questions.explain: An ADR captures the decision and its reasoning so it outlives the person who made it, and gets enforced consistently through review.
